    AI Overview
    The March 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed inflation accelerating to 3.3% annually and 0.9% monthly, the highest levels since May 2024, driven primarily by a 21.2% surge in gasoline prices due to the Iran conflict. Core inflation (excluding food and energy) rose 0.2% monthly and 2.6% annually. 
    Key Findings from March 2026 Report 
    • Annual Inflation: 3.3% for the 12 months ending in March, up from 2.4% in February.
    • Monthly Inflation: 0.9% for March (seasonally adjusted), a significant increase from 0.3% in February.
    • Energy Prices: Gasoline prices surged by 21.2%, representing the largest monthly increase since 1967.
    • Core CPI: Rose 0.2% month-over-month and 2.6% year-over-year.
    • Sector Impact: Airline fares rose 2.7%, while medical care decreased 0.2%. 
    Key Drivers
    The primary driver of the March inflation spike was surging energy costs linked to the conflict with Iran, which tightened the global oil supply. 
    Market Reaction
    Despite the high inflation reading, stocks rose on Friday, with the Nasdaq up 0.35% and the S&P 500 falling 0.11% as investors reacted to the report. 
    For the complete official data, you can review the full Consumer Price Index - March 2026 from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The next report is scheduled for May 12, 2026.

    Limitations. What are the limitations of the CPI?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The Consumer Price Index (CPI) limitations include substitution bias (ignoring consumers switching to cheaper goods), failure to immediately incorporate new products, and difficulty accounting for quality improvements (treating higher quality as pure inflation). Additionally, it uses a fixed basket of goods, often ignoring regional differences and specific demographic spending habits. 
    Key limitations of the CPI include:
    • Substitution Bias:
      When prices rise, consumers buy less of that item and switch to alternatives. Because the CPI basket is fixed, it fails to account for this change, leading to an overstatement of the cost of living. 
    • New Product Introduction:
      The CPI is slow to add new products to its basket, meaning it may miss price declines in new technologies (e.g., streaming services) or fail to capture the convenience they bring until much later. 
    • Unmeasured Quality Change:
      If a product increases in price but also increases in quality, the CPI may count the entire price rise as inflation, even though the consumer is receiving a better product. 
    • Fixed Basket Method:
      The CPI does not track everything; it focuses on a "representative" basket of urban consumer goods. This may not accurately reflect the buying habits of specific groups, such as the elderly or rural residents. 
    • Measurement Errors:
      The index is based on survey samples rather than a full census of all transactions, leading to potential sampling inaccuracies. 
    • Exclusion of Assets:
      The CPI covers consumer goods and services but generally excludes investment items like stocks, bonds, and real estate, which are major components of wealth. 
    Note: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) uses an experimental "geometric mean" formula to help reduce substitution bias.

      Types. What are the different types of CPI?
      About this result
      Feedback
      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) primarily publishes two main Consumer Price Indices: the CPI-U (All Urban Consumers) and CPI-W (Urban Wage Earners). The CPI-U is the broadest measure, covering ~90% of the U.S. population, while the CPI-W covers ~30% and is used to adjust Social Security benefits. 
      Key Types of CPI:
      • CPI-U (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers):
        Represents over 90% of the U.S. population, including professionals, the self-employed, and the unemployed. 
      • CPI-W (Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers):
        A subset of the CPI-U, representing households where more than half of income comes from clerical or wage occupations. 
      • C-CPI-U (Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers):
        A chained version of the CPI-U that accounts for the fact that consumers change their purchasing habits in response to price changes (substitution). 
      • Core CPI (All Items Less Food and Energy):
        Excludes volatile food and energy prices to provide a more stable, long-term picture of underlying inflation. 
      • Specialized/Research Indices (R-CPI-E, etc.):
        Alternative indexes designed for specific groups, such as the R-CPI-E for Americans 62 years of age and older, and various sub-indices for regional or product-specific data. 
      These indices are further broken down by region and item categories (e.g., food, shelter, energy).

        Calculation. How is the CPI calculated?
        About this result
        Feedback
        An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
        AI Overview
        The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is calculated by measuring the weighted average change in prices of a fixed "basket" of goods and services over time. The formula is: (Cost of Market Basket in Current Year ÷ Cost of Market Basket in Base Year) × 100. It involves selecting items, collecting price data monthly, and weighting them by consumer expenditure. 
        Key Steps in Calculation:
        • Define the Basket:
          The BLS identifies a "market basket" of goods and services commonly purchased by urban consumers, including housing (approx. 41%), food, transportation, and medical care. 
        • Collect Prices:
          Over 100,000 prices are collected monthly from retail stores, websites, and service providers. 
        • Calculate Weighted Average:
          Prices are not averaged equally; they are weighted according to their importance in consumer spending. 
        • Calculate the Index:
          The cost of this basket in the current period is divided by the cost in a base period (currently 1982-1984 = 100) and multiplied by 100. 
        CPI Formula in Practice:
        CPI=(Cost of Basket in Current YearCost of Basket in Base Year)×100CPI equals open paren the fraction with numerator Cost of Basket in Current Year and denominator Cost of Basket in Base Year end-fraction close paren cross 100
        For example, if a basket cost
        $100$ 100
        in the base year and
        $250$ 250
        today, the CPI is
        (250100)×100=250open paren 250 over 100 end-fraction close paren cross 100 equals 250
        .         
        Common Formulas Used: 
        • Geometric Mean:
          Most items use a weighted geometric mean of price ratios to account for consumer substitution between items.
        • Modified Laspeyres:
          A weighted arithmetic mean is used for certain items, such as shelter and utilities.
        The inflation rate is then calculated by finding the percentage change in the CPI from one period to another.

          Comparison. How does the CPI compare to other inflation measures?
          Feedback
          The CPI doesn't account for savings, investments, or foreign visitor spending. The Producer Price Index (PPI) measures inflation based on domestic output of raw goods and services. The GDP deflator reflects changes in all goods' and services' prices, without relying on a fixed basket.

          Components. What are the components of the CPI?
          Feedback
          The CPI represents changes in prices of all goods and services purchased for consumption by urban households. User fees (such as water and sewer service) and sales and excise taxes paid by the consumer are also included. Income taxes and investment items (like stocks, bonds, and life insurance) are not included.Sep 9, 2024
